ref: Bavli Yevamot 24a (baraita on Deut 25:6; Gemara; Rava), lines 5-9 of the Wikisource folio
quote_orig: גמ׳ ת"ר (דברים כה, ו) והיה הבכור מיכן שמצוה בגדול לייבם (דברים כה, ו) אשר תלד פרט לאילונית שאין יולדת יקום על שם אחיו לנחלה אתה אומר לנחלה או אינו אלא לשם יוסף קורין אותו יוסף יוחנן קורין אותו יוחנן נאמר כאן יקום על שם אחיו ונאמר להלן (בראשית מח, ו) על שם אחיהם יקראו בנחלתם מה שם האמור להלן נחלה אף שם האמור כאן לנחלה ולא ימחה שמו פרט לסריס ששמו מחוי אמר רבא אע"ג דבכל התורה כולה אין מקרא יוצא מידי פשוטו הכא אתאי גזרה שוה אפיקתיה מפשטיה לגמרי ואי לאו גזרה שוה הוה אמינא שם שם ממש למאן קמזהר רחמנא ליבם יקום על שם אחיך מיבעי ליה אי לבי דינא יקום על שם אחי אביו מיבעי ליה
own_translation_en: Our Rabbis taught: 'And it shall be, the firstborn' - from here: the commandment of levirate marriage falls on the elder brother. 'That she bears' - excluding one who cannot bear. 'Shall arise in the name of his brother' - for inheritance (lanachalah). Do you say it is for inheritance, or only for the name? [If the dead man was called] Yosef, they call him Yosef; [if] Yochanan, they call him Yochanan. It says 'shall arise in the name of his brother' here, and it says there (Gen 48:6) 'in the name of their brothers they shall be called in their inheritance' - just as 'name' there is for inheritance, so 'name' here is for inheritance. Rava said: although in the whole Torah no verse goes out from its plain sense, here a gezerah shavah came and took it entirely out of its plain sense. And had there been no gezerah shavah, I would have said: a name, a name in the literal sense.
licence_note: Hebrew from Sefaria "Wikisource Talmud Bavli", licence CC-BY-SA (page metadata). English is the team's own translation (no public-domain English located).
what_it_shows: The baraita says the phrase "shall arise in the name of his brother" (Deut 25:6) means "for inheritance" (lanachalah), by a gezerah shavah from Gen 48:6, and Rava says this takes the verse entirely out of its plain sense. The Gemara then asks whether the firstborn who performs levirate takes the inheritance, and frames its answer around the one who "arose" (the yavam), not around the child.
context: The Gemara opens with the Mishnah "the commandment of levirate marriage devolves on the elder brother; if the younger forestalled him, he has the right" (Yevamot 24a, Wikisource line 4) and then asks why the verse says "the firstborn". It is a rabbinic exegetical argument, not a legal statement about adoption.
limits: (1) Rava's own words (line 8): though no verse departs from its plain sense, here the gezerah shavah takes it 'entirely' out of its plain sense; line 9: without the gezerah shavah the plain sense would be 'a name in the literal sense'. (2) In line 19 the Gemara's question is about the firstborn who performs levirate ('when the firstborn performs yibbum, should he take the inheritance?') and the answer is framed as 'shall arise ... and here he has arisen', i.e. the one who performs levirate is the subject, not the child. (3) Line 13: a proposed reading that the verse excludes the 'firstborn of the mother' is rejected because 'inheritance (in levirate) is from the father and not from the mother'. (4) Tosafot, Yevamot 24a s.v. 'או אינו אלא לשם' (Vilna ed., Sefaria, public domain; read), says the verse can only be explained of the yavam: 'ליכא לאוקומי קרא אלא ביבם' (the verse cannot be established except regarding the yavam). (5) Yevamot 40a (Wikisource line 23): the Gemara asks whether the Torah tied yibbum to inheritance and answers that they perform yibbum and 'if there is inheritance they take it, and if not, they do not take'. (6) Yevamot 39b: Abba Shaul (minority) considers the child of a levirate marriage made for improper motives a mamzer, i.e. the child is treated as the yavam's offspring for legitimacy (see E-11).
stance: reporting (primary text; the gezerah shavah and Rava are the Gemara's own argument)
to: על שם אחי אביו מיבעי ליה

ref: Antiquities of the Jews, Book IV, ch. 8, sec. 23 (Whiston paragraph numbering)
quote_en: If a woman's husband die, and leave her without children, let his brother marry her, and let him call the son that is born to him by his brother's name, and educate him as the heir of his inheritance, for this procedure will be for the benefit of the public, because thereby families will not fail, and the estate will continue among the kindred;
licence_note: Whiston (1737) translation, Project Gutenberg eBook #2848; Gutenberg boilerplate: "public domain in the United States". Greek not read.
keys: educate him as the heir of his inheritance
call the son that is born to him by his brother's name
the estate will continue among the kindred
what_it_shows: Josephus restates the levirate law as a rule that the brother "shall call the son that is born to him by his brother's name, and educate him as the heir of his inheritance". The source says the child, though born to the brother, is called by the dead man's name and educated as heir of the dead man's inheritance.
context: Josephus (1st c. CE, Jewish historian writing for Greek and Roman readers) paraphrases Deut 25:5-10 as law in his list of Mosaic laws. It is his summary of the statute, not a court record.
limits: (1) Rabbinic sources read the inheritance differently: Mishnah Yevamot 4:7 (E-05) gives the brother who performs levirate the estate; Sifrei Devarim 289:3 (E-04) and Rashi Deut 25:6 (E-10) say the one who performs levirate receives the dead brother's share. Josephus's 'heir' is the child, so the sources disagree on who inherits. (2) In Josephus's own Ruth narrative (Antiquities Book V ch. 9 para. 4) Josephus does not present the child as Mahlon's son; he says Booz married Ruth, and they had a son within a year's time. and that Naomi and the women named him Obed. (3) Josephus gives the rationale 'for the benefit of the public... the estate will continue among the kindred'; this is a policy reason, not a text of Deut 25.
stance: reporting (Josephus restating Mosaic law; not a legal text of the rabbis)
from_: If a woman's husband die, and
to: estate will continue among the kindred;

ref: Ruth 4:9-10 (Boaz to the elders and people)
quote_orig: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ בֹּ֨עַז לַזְּקֵנִ֜ים וְכָל־הָעָ֗ם עֵדִ֤ים אַתֶּם֙ הַיּ֔וֹם כִּ֤י קָנִ֙יתִי֙ אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֶֽאֱלִימֶ֔לֶךְ וְאֵ֛ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְכִלְי֖וֹן וּמַחְל֑וֹן מִיַּ֖ד נָעֳמִֽי׃ וְגַ֣ם אֶת־ר֣וּת הַמֹּאֲבִיָּה֩ אֵ֨שֶׁת מַחְל֜וֹן קָנִ֧יתִי לִ֣י לְאִשָּׁ֗ה לְהָקִ֤ים שֵׁם־הַמֵּת֙ עַל־נַ֣חֲלָת֔וֹ וְלֹא־יִכָּרֵ֧ת שֵׁם־הַמֵּ֛ת מֵעִ֥ם אֶחָ֖יו וּמִשַּׁ֣עַר מְקוֹמ֑וֹ עֵדִ֥ים אַתֶּ֖ם הַיּֽוֹם׃
quote_en: And Boaz said unto the elders, and unto all the people: ‘Ye are witnesses this day, that I have bought all that was Elimelech’s, and all that was Chilion’s and Mahlon’s, of the hand of Naomi. Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I acquired to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place; ye are witnesses this day.’
licence_note: Hebrew: Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra, Public Domain (Sefaria heLicense). English: JPS 1917, Public Domain (Sefaria license).
keys: to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance
that the name of the dead be not cut off
I have bought all that was Elimelech
what_it_shows: Boaz states that he acquires Ruth "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" so that "the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren". The text assigns the child's name and the dead man's inheritance to the purpose of the marriage, without saying the child is biologically Mahlon's.
context: Boaz, the redeemer of Elimelech's land, is buying the field and the widow of Mahlon before the elders at the gate (Ruth 4:1-10). The purpose clause is part of the legal statement of the redemption.
limits: (1) Ruth 4:13: 'So Boaz took Ruth... he went in unto her... and she bore a son', with no statement of Mahlon's paternity. (2) Ruth 4:21: 'and Salmon begot Boaz, and Boaz begot Obed'; the genealogy traces Obed through Boaz, not Mahlon (see E-07). (3) Ruth 4:6: the nearer kinsman refuses 'lest I mar mine own inheritance'; this is usually read as the fear that a child of Ruth would take the field, but the text does not say the child is counted as Mahlon's son for lineage. (4) Josephus (Ant 5.9.4, E-02) and Matthew 1:5 (E-08) both name Boaz as Obed's begetter.
from_: And Boaz said unto the elders,
to: place; ye are witnesses this day.’

ref: Sifrei Devarim 289:3 on Deut 25:6 ("shall arise in the name of his brother")
quote_orig: יקום על שם אחיו. (ולא על שם אחי אביו.) [לנחלה. נאמר כאן "שם אחיו", ונאמר להלן "על שם אחיהם יקראו בנחלתם". מה "שם" האמור להלן, לנחלה; אף "שם" האמור כאן, לנחלה].
quote_en: (The yavam) "shall be invested in the name of his dead brother": for inheritance (i.e., he receives his dead brother's share as well as his own.) It is written here "in the name of his brother," and, elsewhere (Bereshith 48:6) "in the name of their brothers (Ephraim and Menasheh) shall they be called in (taking) their inheritance." Just as there, the reference is to taking inheritance, so, here.
licence_note: Hebrew: "Sifrei Devarim, Hebrew" Public Domain (Sefaria). English: Silverstein, CC-BY (Sefaria). The parentheses and brackets are as printed on those pages; the bracket around the English parenthetical "(The yavam)" is the translator's insertion.
what_it_shows: Sifrei reads "shall arise in the name of his brother" as "for inheritance" (lanachalah), using Gen 48:6 ("in the name of their brothers they shall be called in their inheritance") as the comparison. In the English of Silverstein the one who receives the share is the yavam, not the child.
context: Tannaitic midrash on the levirate chapter (Deut 25:5-10), one of the sources quoted in Yevamot 24a. It is a halakhic reading of the verse.
limits: (1) The English 'shall be invested... (The yavam) ... he receives his dead brother's share as well as his own' is Silverstein's text; the parenthesis '(The yavam)' is his insertion, not in the Hebrew of line 3. The Hebrew line itself says only 'for inheritance'. (2) Sifrei 289:9 (Hebrew): R. Yehuda compares 'name' here with 'name' in Num 27:4 (daughters of Zelophehad). The printed Hebrew carries two variant readings in parentheses and brackets, one ending 'for inheritance' (nachalah) and one 'seed' (zera); Silverstein's English follows 'seed'. The variants are as printed on Sefaria and were not checked against a critical edition. (3) Sifrei 289:1 (same page): 'yakum al shem achiv' is read as the dead brother's name and not the father's brother's name; the child is named after the dead man. (4) Rashi and Yevamot 24a (E-01, E-10) read the same clause as the yavam's share.
to: is to taking inheritance, so, here.

quote_orig: החולץ ליבמתו הרי הוא כאחד מן האחין לנחלה. ואם יש שם אב נכסים של אב. הכונס את יבמתו. זכה בנכסים של אחיו.
quote_en: He who performs halitzah with his yevamah, behold he is regarded as one of the other brothers in respect of inheritance. If the father was living, the estate belongs to the father. He who marries his yevamah acquires his brother’s estate. R. Judah said: in either case, if the father was living the estate belongs to the father.
licence_note: Hebrew: Romm Vilna 1913, Public Domain (Sefaria). English: Mishnah Yomit by Dr. Joshua Kulp, CC-BY (Sefaria). Danby/Blackman not used.
keys: ואם יש שם אב נכסים של אב
what_it_shows: The Mishnah says the brother who performs levirate with the widow "acquires his brother's estate", and that the brother who performs chalitzah is "like one of the brothers" for inheritance. In both cases the inheritance goes to a brother, not to a child, and if the father is living the estate goes to the father.
context: Mishnah Yevamot 4:7 states the property rights of the yavam (levir) and of the chalitzah brother; the Gemara on Yevamot 40a discusses this same mishnah (Wikisource line 12).
limits: (1) This Mishnah assigns the estate to the yavam (the surviving brother), not to a levirate child, which is the reverse of the thesis. (2) The father of the deceased takes precedence: 'if there is a father, the property belongs to the father' (both the chalitzah and yibbum cases). (3) R. Yehuda's view (same mishnah): 'in either case, if the father was living the estate belongs to the father' (same rule, no difference). (4) Mishnah Bekhorot 8:9 (English CC0, Sefaria Community Translation, read): 'nor the yavam, none of them take a double portion' (the yavam gets no double portion). (5) Mishnah Yevamot 2 and 6 scanned in Hebrew for inheritance/name terms: none found. Yevamot 40a (Wikisource line 23) asks whether the Torah tied yibbum to inheritance and answers that they perform yibbum and take the inheritance only if there is one.
from_: He who performs halitzah with his
to: the estate belongs to the father.

quote_orig: כִּֽי־יֵשְׁב֨וּ אַחִ֜ים יַחְדָּ֗ו וּמֵ֨ת אַחַ֤ד מֵהֶם֙ וּבֵ֣ן אֵֽין־ל֔וֹ לֹֽא־תִהְיֶ֧ה אֵֽשֶׁת־הַמֵּ֛ת הַח֖וּצָה לְאִ֣ישׁ זָ֑ר יְבָמָהּ֙ יָבֹ֣א עָלֶ֔יהָ וּלְקָחָ֥הּ ל֛וֹ לְאִשָּׁ֖ה וְיִבְּמָֽהּ׃ וְהָיָ֗ה הַבְּכוֹר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֵּלֵ֔ד יָק֕וּם עַל־שֵׁ֥ם אָחִ֖יו הַמֵּ֑ת וְלֹֽא־יִמָּחֶ֥ה שְׁמ֖וֹ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
quote_en: If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not be married abroad unto one not of his kin; her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother unto her. And it shall be, that the first-born that she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother that is dead, that his name be not blotted out of Israel.
licence_note: Hebrew: Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra, Public Domain (Sefaria). English: JPS 1917, Public Domain (Sefaria).
what_it_shows: The verse says that the first-born whom the widow bears "shall succeed in the name of his brother that is dead, that his name be not blotted out of Israel". The text speaks of the dead man's name, and does not mention inheritance or blood.
context: The levirate law of Deut 25:5-10. The first-born is the child the widow bears to the levir; the verse is the Pentateuchal basis for the rabbinic debate in E-01.
limits: (1) The verse itself mentions only 'name', not 'inheritance' or 'lineage'; the inheritance reading comes from the gezerah shavah with Gen 48:6 (E-01, E-04). (2) Rava: the plain sense is 'a name in the literal sense' (Yevamot 24a, E-01). (3) Onkelos (Aramaic, Public Domain on Sefaria; read): 'על שְׁמָא דַאֲחוּהִי מֵתָנָא' - 'upon the name of his dead brother', with no inheritance word. (4) Sifrei 289:9: R. Yehuda reads 'name' as 'seed' (zera) (E-04). (5) Deut 25:5: the wife 'shall not be married abroad' (Hebrew 'החוצה לאיש זר') and the brother 'shall go in unto her'; the law is for brothers who 'dwell together'.

to: be not blotted out of Israel.

ref: Ruth 4:17-21 (the women name the child; genealogy from Perez to David)
quote_orig: וַתִּקְרֶאנָה֩ ל֨וֹ הַשְּׁכֵנ֥וֹת שֵׁם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר יֻלַּד־בֵּ֖ן לְנָעֳמִ֑י וַתִּקְרֶ֤אנָֽה שְׁמוֹ֙ עוֹבֵ֔ד ה֥וּא אֲבִי־יִשַׁ֖י אֲבִ֥י דָוִֽד׃ (פ) וְאֵ֙לֶּה֙ תּוֹלְד֣וֹת פָּ֔רֶץ פֶּ֖רֶץ הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־חֶצְרֽוֹן׃ וְחֶצְרוֹן֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־רָ֔ם וְרָ֖ם הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־עַמִּֽינָדָֽב׃ וְעַמִּֽינָדָב֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־נַחְשׁ֔וֹן וְנַחְשׁ֖וֹן הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־שַׂלְמָֽה׃ וְשַׂלְמוֹן֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־בֹּ֔עַז וּבֹ֖עַז הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־עוֹבֵֽד׃
quote_en: And the women her neighbours gave it a name, saying: ‘There is a son born to Naomi’; and they called his name Obed; he is the father of Jesse, the father of David. Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez begot Hezron; and Hezron begot Ram, and Ram begot Amminadab; and Amminadab begot Nahshon, and Nahshon begot Salmon; and Salmon begot Boaz, and Boaz begot Obed;
licence_note: Hebrew: Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra, Public Domain (Sefaria). English: JPS 1917, Public Domain (Sefaria).
what_it_shows: The neighbours name the child "There is a son born to Naomi" (a naming by the community), but the genealogy then reads "Salmon begot Boaz, and Boaz begot Obed" and traces Obed to Perez and David through Boaz, not through Mahlon. The genealogy therefore reckons Obed through Boaz.
context: Closing section of Ruth, after the marriage and the birth; the genealogy of David (Ruth 4:18-22) follows the naming.
limits: (1) Ruth 4:21 names Boaz as the begetter of Obed, so the genealogy in Ruth does NOT list Mahlon as Obed's father. (2) The naming in 4:17 is by the neighbouring women and calls the child 'born to Naomi', not Mahlon's son; the text describes no legal act of adoption. (3) Matthew 1:5 (E-08) also has Boaz as the begetter of Obed.

ref: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History I.7.2 (quoting Julius Africanus, Letter to Aristides)
quote_en: For whereas the names of the generations were reckoned in Israel either according to nature or according to law — according to nature by the succession of legitimate offspring, and according to law whenever another raised up a child to the name of a brother dying childless; for because a clear hope of resurrection was not yet given they had a representation of the future promise by a kind of mortal resurrection, in order that the name of the one deceased might be perpetuated —
licence_note: NPNF2-01 (1890), translated by Arthur Cushman McGiffert, as posted at New Advent; the page states the site copyright only, no licence for the translation.
keys: according to law whenever another raised up a child to the name of a brother dying childless
what_it_shows: Africanus (quoted by Eusebius) says that "the names of the generations were reckoned in Israel either according to nature or according to law", and that by law "another raised up a child to the name of a brother dying childless". He presents this as a general account of how generations were reckoned.
context: Africanus, a Christian chronographer, writes to Aristides to reconcile Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Joseph. Eusebius quotes him in Church History I.7, and Eusebius then gives a separate account, handed down by the Lord's relatives, about Herod's ancestry (I.7.11-12).
limits: (1) Africanus's claim is a reconstruction by a Christian writer to harmonise two Gospels; he gives no Hebrew source for 'according to law' in this passage. (2) Africanus's own model (I.7.9): Joseph was Jacob's son 'by nature' and Eli's son 'according to law'; so in his model legal sonship and biological sonship come apart, and the legal father is the dead brother. (3) Africanus's text: 'But according to law he was the son of Eli, for Jacob, being the brother of the latter, raised up seed to him.' - the levirate 'raised up seed' is treated as legal. (4) The text I read does NOT say the levirate explanation came from the Lord's relatives: section 1 says only 'the account which he had received from tradition'; the relatives' account in I.7.11-12 is about Herod's descent from Antipater (Idumean). Eusebius adds 'whether with the desire of boasting or simply wishing to state the fact' about the relatives. (5) I.7.13 (Eusebius, same chapter): the archives had 'the genealogies of the Hebrews as well as of those who traced their lineage back to proselytes, such as Achior the Ammonite and Ruth the Moabitess'; Herod burned them. This is a historical report that Ruth's line was recorded, not a rule about adoption. (6) Rabbinic sources (E-01, E-05) do not make the child heir in the same way; they assign the share to the yavam.
stance: commentator (Christian reconstruction quoted by Eusebius; not a Jewish legal text)

ref: Rashi on Deuteronomy 25:6, third clause ("shall arise in the name of his brother")
quote_orig: יקום על שם אחיו. זֶה שֶׁיִּבֵּם אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ יִטֹּל נַחֲלַת הַמֵּת בְּנִכְסֵי אָבִיו:
quote_en: יקום על שם אחיו HE SHALL SUCCEED IN THE NAME OF HIS BROTHER — he who has married his (the deceased brother’s) wife shall receive the portion of the dead brother in his father’s property (Sifrei Devarim 289:3).
licence_note: Rosenbaum & Silbermann (1929-1934), Public Domain (Sefaria). Hebrew with nikkud as on the page.
what_it_shows: Rashi glosses "shall arise in the name of his brother" as: the one who performed the levirate marriage with the widow takes the dead man's share in the father's property. In Rashi the heir is the yavam, not the child.
context: Rashi (11th c.) comments on the verse; the English on Sefaria cites Sifrei Devarim 289:3 for this clause.
limits: (1) This is the reverse of the thesis: the inheritance goes to the surviving brother who performs levirate, not to the child. (2) Rashi's English (Rosenbaum & Silbermann) gives the same reading: 'he who has married his (the deceased brother's) wife shall receive the portion of the dead brother in his father's property'. (3) Rashi's gloss on 'shall arise in the name of his brother' gives the share (nachalah) to the yavam; it says nothing about the child's lineage.
from_: יקום על שם אחיו HE SHALL

ref: Bavli Yevamot 39b (Abba Shaul, minority opinion on the levirate child)
quote_orig: דתניא אבא שאול אומר הכונס את יבמתו לשם נוי ולשום אישות ולשום דבר אחר כאילו פוגע בערוה וקרוב אני בעיני להיות הולד ממזר וחכמים אומרים (דברים כה, ה) יבמה יבא עליה מכל מקום
own_translation_en: As taught: Abba Shaul says: one who takes his yevamah for beauty, or for the sake of marriage, or for any other purpose, is as one who strikes a forbidden relation; and it seems to me that the child is a mamzer. And the Sages say: 'a yevamah shall come upon her' (Deut 25:5) - in any case.
licence_note: Hebrew: Wikisource Talmud Bavli, CC-BY-SA (Sefaria). English is the team's own translation.
keys: וקרוב אני בעיני להיות הולד ממזר
what_it_shows: Abba Shaul holds that a levirate marriage contracted for improper motives makes the child a mamzer, i.e. the child is treated as the yavam's own offspring for legitimacy. This is a statement about status, not about lineage or inheritance.
context: Discussion of who may perform yibbum and when it is forbidden; the Sages' view is the one the Gemara adopts (Yevamot 39b, 40a).
limits: (1) Abba Shaul is a minority opinion: the Sages reject it and read 'a yevamah shall come upon her' in any case. (2) The statement concerns legitimacy (mamzer status), not lineage; it does not say the child inherits the dead brother's name or share. (3) Yevamot 22b (Wikisource line 6, read): a son, even a mamzer, exempts from levirate; this concerns the status of a son for the levirate rule, not adoption.
stance: reporting (minority opinion, quoted in the Gemara)
from_: דתניא אבא שאול אומר הכונס את
to: ה) יבמה יבא עליה מכל מקום

ref: Genesis 38:8-9 (Judah to Onan; Onan spills his seed)
quote_orig: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוּדָה֙ לְאוֹנָ֔ן בֹּ֛א אֶל־אֵ֥שֶׁת אָחִ֖יךָ וְיַבֵּ֣ם אֹתָ֑הּ וְהָקֵ֥ם זֶ֖רַע לְאָחִֽיךָ׃ וַיֵּ֣דַע אוֹנָ֔ן כִּ֛י לֹּ֥א ל֖וֹ יִהְיֶ֣ה הַזָּ֑רַע וְהָיָ֞ה אִם־בָּ֨א אֶל־אֵ֤שֶׁת אָחִיו֙ וְשִׁחֵ֣ת אַ֔רְצָה לְבִלְתִּ֥י נְתָן־זֶ֖רַע לְאָחִֽיו׃
quote_en: And Judah said unto Onan: ‘Go in unto thy brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother unto her, and raise up seed to thy brother.’ And Onan knew that the seed would not be his; and it came to pass when he went in unto his brother’s wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest he should give seed to his brother.
licence_note: Hebrew: Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra, Public Domain (Sefaria). English: JPS 1917, Public Domain (Sefaria).
keys: the seed would not be his
what_it_shows: Judah tells Onan to "raise up seed to your brother", and the narrator says Onan knew "the seed would not be his". The narrator says Onan knew the seed would not count as his own, which shows that the offspring of the levirate was understood not to be the living brother's; the text does not say to whom in law it belongs.
context: The earliest levirate case in the Torah (Gen 38:8-10), the story of Judah, Tamar, Er and Onan. No name, inheritance or adoption term appears.
limits: (1) Gen 38 does not use the words 'name' or 'inheritance'; it says 'raise up seed to your brother' only. (2) The text presents the levirate as Judah's command to Onan, not as a rule about lineage for the child's whole life. (3) Gen 38:11: Judah sends Tamar back to her father's house until Shelah 'be grown up', so the levirate with Shelah is deferred, not carried out.
to: should give seed to his brother.
